title: Scoring a Run: Navigation, Manipulation and Gait Metrics, and Criteria That Turn Numbers Into a Pass or a Fail

questions.question: Why is reached the goal not a score?
options: It says nothing about the way there: collisions, time, rhythm
It cannot be computed from a log
It is true of every run
It depends on the log's rate
questions.explanation: Two runs that both arrive can differ in everything that matters: one clean and quick, the other through two posts and twice as long.

questions.question: A V shaped detour, 2 m off a 10 m line, had a straightness of:
questions.explanation: The straight distance over the distance walked: 10 m over 10.77 m. A straight run scores 1.

questions.question: Why are collisions counted as events?
options: Events are easier to draw
A sample cannot be inside an obstacle
To make the score larger
Samples inside an obstacle depend on the log's rate, not on the mistake
questions.explanation: Driving through two posts was 110 samples and two mistakes. At twice the logging rate it would be 220 samples and still two.

questions.question: 20 trials with two failures gave a success rate of:
options: 80.0 percent
95.0 percent
90.0 percent
18 percent
questions.explanation: Eighteen of twenty succeeded. The failed trials count against the rate and are left out of the times.

questions.question: The mean time was 4.72 s and the 95th percentile 9.00 s. Which matters to a cell with a deadline?
options: The mean, which uses every trial
The fastest trial
The 95th percentile, which shows the slow ones
The success rate alone
questions.explanation: One slow trial pulled the 95th percentile to 9.00 s while the mean stayed at 4.72 s. A cycle time is broken by the slow ones.

questions.question: What does the irregularity of a gait measure?
options: The fraction of time a foot is down
The spread of the stride periods over their mean
How fast the robot walks
The length of a stride
questions.explanation: A steady gait gave 0.000 and one with a single missed step 0.222.
